en: To accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest
hook: ACQUIESCE: 'ACQUI-YES', saying a quiet yes.
story: Acquiesce. To accept something reluctantly, but without protest. Nadia had planned a quiet wedding with twenty guests. Her mother had other plans: a big community centre in Uttara, four hundred guests, and a holud night with a live band. Nadia opened her mouth to argue, looked at her mother's shining eyes, [sigh] and closed it again. She acquiesced. Inside acquiesce is the Latin quies, meaning rest, the same root as quiet: to acquiesce is to accept quietly, without a fight. So, what verb means to go along with something you would not have chosen, without protest? ... Acquiesce.

gre.s: Although she privately opposed the merger, the director chose to ____ rather than risk a damaging public battle with the board.
gre.clue: rather than risk a damaging public battle

example: Tired of arguing, the residents' committee acquiesced to the developer's plan to cut down two old mango trees.

en: To choose someone ceremonially for a role; to apply oil as part of a religious ceremony
bn: অভিষিক্ত করা; উত্তরাধিকারী হিসেবে মনোনীত করা
hook: ANOINT: kings were 'A-OIL-ed' — oil on the head at coronation.
story: Anoint. To choose someone ceremonially for an important role; also, to put oil on someone in a religious ceremony. When Grandfather Habib turned eighty, he gathered the whole family in his famous sweet shop in Natore. Everyone expected his eldest son to take over. Instead, he placed his old brass ladle in the hands of his granddaughter Mitali. [gasp] He had anointed her, just as kings were once anointed with holy oil. Anoint shares its root with ointment, an oily cream rubbed on the skin. So, what verb means to formally choose someone as the next leader? ... Anoint.

gre.s: Although many party insiders expected an open contest, the retiring leader chose to ____ his deputy as successor, effectively ending the race before it began.
gre.clue: effectively ending the race before it began

example: Critics were quick to anoint the young Rajshahi novelist as the most important new voice of her generation.

en: A brief, clever saying that sums up a broad truth
hook: APHORISM: a short AFFIRMATION of truth.
story: Aphorism. A brief, clever saying that sums up a broad truth. Whenever Nafis wasted an afternoon on his phone, his grandmother would say one line in Bangla: an idle mind is the devil's workshop. As a boy, Nafis rolled his eyes at her aphorisms. But years later, during his GRE preparation, he caught himself whispering that same line whenever he felt lazy. Aphorism comes from a Greek word meaning to mark off or define: an aphorism defines a big truth in a few words. So, what word names a short, wise saying that captures a broad truth? ... Aphorism.

gre.s: The essay closes with a single pithy ____, "Certainty ages a face faster than doubt," which has been quoted far more often than any of the arguments that precede it.
gre.clue: a single pithy

example: Sticky notes bearing Tania's favourite aphorism, done is better than perfect, lined the edge of her computer monitor.

en: So confused that you cannot think clearly
hook: BE-FUDDLED: a brain in a MUDDLE.
story: Befuddled. So confused that you cannot think clearly. Rafi's grandfather got his first smartphone last Eid. He pressed one button, and the screen turned sideways. He pressed another, and a video of a dancing cat began to play, loudly, in the middle of dinner. He held the phone at arm's length, completely befuddled, while the grandchildren [laugh] rushed to help. Befuddled rhymes with muddled, and a befuddled mind is exactly that: a muddle where no clear thought can get through. So, what word describes someone so confused they cannot think straight? ... Befuddled.

gre.s: Students left the lecture thoroughly ____, as the professor had jumped between unrelated theories without explaining any of them.
gre.clue: without explaining any of them

example: Jet lag left the visiting scientist so befuddled that she gave her keynote talk with the slides in the wrong order.

en: To give a false impression of; to hide the truth behind an appearance
bn: ভুল ধারণা দেওয়া; আসল রূপ আড়াল করা
hook: BE-LIE: the appearance tells a LIE about what's underneath.
story: Belie. To give a false impression of something; to hide the truth behind an appearance. At her thesis defence, Anika answered every question in a calm, steady voice. The examiners nodded, impressed. Only her best friend, in the back row, could see her fingers twisting the end of her orna under the table. Anika's calm voice belied her racing heart. The trick is in the word itself: be plus lie. When an appearance belies the truth, it tells a lie about what is underneath. So, what verb means to give a false impression of what is really there? ... Belie.

gre.s: The pianist's relaxed, almost careless stage manners ____ the punishing hours of practice that lie behind every performance.
gre.clue: relaxed, almost careless

example: The bakery's tiny, shabby storefront belies the remarkable quality of the pastries made inside.

en: Cheerfully carefree; casually indifferent to something serious
hook: BLITHE: BLISSfully unaware.
story: Blithe. Cheerfully carefree; also, casually unconcerned about something serious. Every morning, Zayan's cousin rides his motorbike through Dhaka traffic without a helmet, humming a song and waving at friends. When his mother begs him to be careful, he only grins. "Nothing will happen to me, Amma." His blithe confidence makes her stomach twist. Blithe can be sweet, like a child's blithe laughter, but on the GRE it often means not worrying when you should. Blithe and bliss are old relatives: a blithe person floats along in blissful unconcern. So, what word describes someone carelessly cheerful about a real danger? ... Blithe.

gre.s: The CEO's ____ dismissal of the auditors' warnings, delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand, alarmed investors who knew how serious the losses were.
gre.clue: delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand

example: Some commuters in Dhaka cross the busy road with blithe disregard for the buses roaring toward them.

en: Cautious; carefully considering all circumstances before acting
hook: CIRCUM-SPECT: looking (spect) all around (circum) before acting.
story: Circumspect. Cautious; carefully considering everything before acting. When a stranger on Facebook offered Imran a well-paid job in Dubai, his friends told him to grab it. Imran was more circumspect. He called the company, asked for its licence, and requested a cousin in Dubai to visit the address. There was no office there at all. [sigh] Being circumspect had saved him. Circum means around, and spect means look, as in spectacles: a circumspect person looks all around before taking a step. So, what word describes someone careful to consider everything before acting? ... Circumspect.

gre.s: Having been burned by a previous scandal, the senator was ____ in her public statements, weighing every word before she spoke.
gre.clue: weighing every word before she spoke

example: Journalists covering the election learned to be circumspect on the phone, assuming that every call might be monitored.

en: To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose
hook: COL-LUDE: playing (ludere) together secretly.
story: Collude. To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose. In a market town in Dinajpur, rice prices jumped in every shop on the same morning. Rubina's father, a schoolteacher, found it strange. A local reporter dug deeper and discovered that the three biggest wholesalers had met at night and agreed to hold back their stock together. They had colluded to squeeze every family in town. Collude comes from the Latin for playing together, the same root as ludicrous: those who collude play a secret game against everyone else. So, what verb means to work together secretly to cheat others? ... Collude.

gre.s: Investigators suspected that the two rival bidders had secretly agreed to ____, inflating their offers so that the government would pay far more than the project was worth.
gre.clue: secretly agreed

example: Officials found that several exam invigilators had colluded with a printing press to leak the question papers.

en: Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done wrong
hook: CONTRITE: sounds like 'contrition' — a confession full of regret.
story: Contrite. Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done wrong. Playing cricket in the lane, eleven-year-old Shafin hit a six straight through old Rahela Nani's window. The other boys ran. Shafin did not. He knocked on her door, eyes on the floor, holding out the ball and his whole month's pocket money. "I am really sorry, Nani." His voice shook. She looked at the contrite boy, [chuckle] and offered him a biscuit. Contrite comes from the Latin for crushed: a contrite heart feels crushed by guilt. So, what word describes someone full of genuine regret for a wrong? ... Contrite.

gre.s: The defendant's ____ statement, in which he tearfully apologized to the victims, persuaded the judge to reduce his sentence.
gre.clue: tearfully apologized to the victims

example: The contrite striker visited the injured defender in hospital and apologized for his reckless tackle.

en: A formal or authoritative statement; a short saying
hook: DICTUM: what is DICTATED, spoken (dictus).
story: Dictum. A formal, authoritative statement; also, a short saying. At Rahim's school in Sirajganj, the headmaster had one famous dictum, painted above the gate: "Discipline is the bridge between goals and success." Every morning for ten years, students walked under it. Today, as a busy doctor, Rahim repeats that dictum to his young interns, and they roll their eyes exactly the way he once did. Dictum comes from the Latin dicere, to say, as in dictate and dictionary: a dictum is something said with authority. So, what word names an authoritative statement or principle? ... Dictum.

gre.s: The founder's ____ that the customer is always right was treated by her managers as an unquestionable law, though she herself frequently ignored it.
gre.clue: treated by her managers as an unquestionable law

example: Architects still quote the famous dictum that form follows function, though few of their buildings actually obey it.

en: To extract the essential meaning; to purify a liquid by heating
hook: DISTILL: boil it down to the pure essence.
story: Distill. To extract the essential meaning of something; also, to purify a liquid by heating and cooling it. In chemistry lab, Priya watched muddy water boil in a flask, while clean drops slowly gathered in a cool glass tube on the other side. Years later, her boss handed her a two-hundred-page report and asked for one page by morning. She worked all night and distilled it to its pure essence. It felt just like the lab: boil away everything else and keep only what matters. So, what verb means to boil something down to its essential meaning? ... Distill.

gre.s: In just a few pages, the author manages to ____ decades of complex research into a handful of clear principles that any reader can grasp.
gre.clue: into a handful of clear principles

example: Before kickoff, the coach distilled the whole match plan into three words on the whiteboard: press, pass, shoot.

en: To gradually intrude beyond proper limits
hook: EN-CROACH: like a COCKROACH creeping into your space.
story: Encroach. To gradually intrude beyond proper limits. When Kamal's grandfather was young, the canal behind their Dhaka neighbourhood was wide enough for boats. Then, year by year, people began to encroach on it: first a bamboo platform, then a tin shed, then a concrete wall. Today the canal is a thin, black drain, and the old man still points to where the water once shone. Encroach comes from an old French word for hook: those who encroach hook a little more space each time. So, what verb means to creep beyond your proper limits? ... Encroach.

gre.s: Residents worried that the expanding city would gradually ____ on the surrounding farmland, swallowing a few more fields each year until none remained.
gre.clue: swallowing a few more fields each year

example: Long working hours began to encroach on the evenings Babul had promised to spend with his children.

en: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective
hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
story: Feckless. Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective. Ruma's uncle has started six businesses in ten years, from a phone shop to a poultry farm. Each one failed within months, because he slept till noon and let his friends run up unpaid bills. Now he asks Ruma's father for money again, smiling as if nothing happened. The family loves him, but everyone agrees he is feckless. Feck is an old Scottish word for effect, so a feckless person is one without effect, achieving nothing. So, what word describes someone weak-willed and irresponsible? ... Feckless.

gre.s: Voters grew frustrated with the ____ government, which announced ambitious plans every year but never carried any of them out.
gre.clue: never carried any of them out

example: Her feckless brother borrowed money to start a new business every year and lost it within months.

en: Fussy and hard to please; requiring great attention to detail
hook: FINICKY: FINE details only — picky.
story: Finicky. Fussy and hard to please; also, needing great attention to detail. Seven-year-old Ayaan will eat rice only if the dal does not touch it. His egg must be fried, never boiled, and the onion must be invisible. If a single curry leaf appears on his plate, he pushes it away with one finger, and his mother [sigh] picks it out, every time. Ayaan is the most finicky eater in the family. Finicky sounds like fine plus picky, and a finicky person fusses over every fine detail. So, what word describes someone fussy and hard to please? ... Finicky.

gre.s: The critic was notoriously ____ about food, sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool or whose garnish sat slightly off centre.
gre.clue: sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool

example: Orchids are finicky plants, so my aunt in Mymensingh checks the humidity in her greenhouse twice a day.

en: Secretive and sly, as if trying to avoid notice
hook: FURTIVE: like a FERRET, sneaking around quietly.
story: Furtive. Secretive and sly, as if trying to avoid notice. In the exam hall, the invigilator walked slowly between the rows. One boy near the window kept stealing quick, furtive glances at his left sleeve, then back at his paper, then at the invigilator. The invigilator stopped beside him, gently turned back the sleeve, and found tiny notes written in ink. [gasp] The boy's face went pale. Furtive comes from the Latin fur, meaning thief: a furtive look is the quick glance of a thief. So, what word describes a secretive glance meant to avoid notice? ... Furtive.

gre.s: The thief cast ____ glances around the gallery before slipping the small sculpture into his coat.
gre.clue: before slipping the small sculpture into his coat

example: The two lovers exchanged furtive smiles across the crowded wedding hall, careful that no relative noticed.

en: Rude and cheeky in a bold, shameless way
hook: IM-PUDENT: no shame (pudor = shame).
story: Impudent. Rude and cheeky in a bold, shameless way. In a long bank queue in Motijheel, a young man walked straight to the counter and pushed his cheque in front of an old woman. When the clerk asked him to wait his turn, he smirked. "Make me." Shamima, standing behind the old woman, could hardly believe such impudent behaviour. The whole queue stared until he stepped back. Inside impudent is the Latin pudor, shame, and im means without: an impudent person has no shame at all. So, what word describes someone rude and shamelessly bold? ... Impudent.

gre.s: The ____ student not only ignored the teacher's warning but mimicked her voice in front of the whole class, apparently without the slightest shame.
gre.clue: apparently without the slightest shame

example: An impudent post from the club's official account mocked the referee and earned the team a heavy fine.

en: So clearly true that no one can argue against it
hook: IN-CONTROVERT-IBLE: NO CONTROVERSY possible.
story: Incontrovertible. So clearly true that no one can argue against it. Two neighbours in Banani argued for a week about who had scratched a new car in their garage. Each blamed the other's driver. Then the building guard quietly brought the security camera footage. On the screen, clear as day, a delivery van backed into the car and drove away. The argument ended in an instant. The video was incontrovertible proof. Break it apart: in means not, and controvert means argue against, as in controversy, so incontrovertible means beyond argument. So, what word describes evidence no one can dispute? ... Incontrovertible.

gre.s: Although the theory was once fiercely contested, the satellite data now provide ____ proof, leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt.
gre.clue: leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt

example: Carbon dating of the paper gave the museum incontrovertible proof that its prized manuscript was a modern forgery.

en: Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering
hook: MAGISTERIAL: like a MAGISTRATE in court.
story: Magisterial. Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering. When the family gathered to settle a quarrel over land, nobody spoke until Nayeem's grandmother entered. She sat at the head of the table, adjusted her glasses, and listened to each son in turn. Then she gave her decision in three calm sentences. No one argued. Her magisterial presence filled the room, and even her silence was magisterial. Think of a magistrate in court: magisterial and magistrate both come from the Latin magister, meaning master. So, what word describes a manner full of commanding authority? ... Magisterial.

gre.s: The historian's ____ survey of the empire, which drew on sources in twelve languages, is still regarded as the definitive work on the subject.
gre.clue: is still regarded as the definitive work

example: The retired judge gave a magisterial lecture on the constitution, speaking for two hours without a single note.

en: Done with minimal effort, routinely and without real interest
hook: PERFUNCTORY: done just to PERFORM the FUNCTION, nothing more.
story: Perfunctory. Done with minimal effort, routinely and without real interest. At the entrance of a big shopping mall in Dhaka, a security guard waves a metal detector near each visitor's bag. The detector beeps for everyone, and he waves everyone through anyway. Rafsan [chuckle] whispers that a tiger could walk past. The check is perfunctory, done only to say it was done. Perfunctory comes from a Latin word for getting a duty over with: a perfunctory task is simply got through, nothing more. So, what word describes a task done routinely, with no real care? ... Perfunctory.

gre.s: The manager gave the report only a ____ glance before signing it, a carelessness that allowed several glaring errors to slip through.
gre.clue: allowed several glaring errors to slip through

example: The waiter's perfunctory smile vanished the moment he turned away from our table.

en: To be the one who commits a crime or wrong
hook: PERPETRATE: a PERP (criminal) does it.
story: Perpetrate. To be the one who commits a crime or a wrong. For weeks, people in Rangpur received calls from a man claiming to work for their mobile banking company, asking for their secret code. Many lost their savings. Then police traced the calls to one small rented room, where two young men sat with a pile of phones. They had perpetrated the entire fraud. Perpetrate comes from a Latin word for carrying out an act, and the one who perpetrates a crime is the perpetrator. So, what verb means to be the one who carries out a wrong? ... Perpetrate.

gre.s: Although the soldiers claimed they were only following orders, the tribunal held that those who ____ such atrocities bear personal responsibility for them.
gre.clue: the soldiers claimed they were only following orders

example: The bank's own IT manager perpetrated the fraud, quietly moving small sums into hidden accounts for six years.

en: Having a sad, longing sound, like a cry or lament
hook: PLAINTIVE: like a PLAINT, a sad complaint.
story: Plaintive. Having a sad, longing sound, like a cry or a lament. On a ferry crossing the Padma at dusk, Ishrat heard an old boatman singing a bhatiali song as he rowed past. His voice rose and fell over the water, slow and aching, a song about a far-off home. Even the children stopped playing to listen. It was the most plaintive sound she had ever heard. Plaintive comes from plaint, an old word for a lament, the same root as complaint. So, what word describes a sad, longing sound, like a boatman's song at dusk? ... Plaintive.

gre.s: From the abandoned house drifted the ____ notes of a flute, so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent.
gre.clue: so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent

example: Through the thin wall we heard the plaintive mewing of the neighbour's kitten, which had been shut out of the kitchen.

en: Strongly critical or controversial in argument
hook: POLEMICAL: POLE-vaulting into a fight; aggressive argument.
story: Polemical. Strongly critical or controversial in argument. Every Friday, a well-known columnist in a Dhaka newspaper writes a fierce attack on someone: a minister, a cricket board, a famous writer. His words are sharp, his tone furious, and readers either cheer or send angry letters. Rubel's father reads each column aloud at breakfast, shaking his head. "Polemical again." Polemical writing goes to war with words, and that is exactly its origin: polemos is the Greek word for war. So, what word describes writing that attacks fiercely and stirs controversy? ... Polemical.

gre.s: Although the book's ____ tone alienated some readers, its fierce attack on the policy succeeded in sparking a national debate.
gre.clue: its fierce attack on the policy

example: The scientist's polemical blog posts against homeopathy won her many fans and a few angry lawsuits.

en: Slow and clumsy because of great weight; dull and laborious
hook: PONDEROUS: as heavy as a POUND of lead.
story: Ponderous. Slow and clumsy because of great weight; also, dull and laborious. At the Narayanganj river port, Rezwan watched an old cargo ship pull away, loaded to the edge with sand. It moved so slowly that a boy on the bank walked faster. That evening, his GRE reading passage felt the same: endless clauses, no life at all. Both were ponderous. Ponderous comes from the Latin pondus, weight, the same root as ponder, to weigh a thought in your mind. So, what word describes something slow and heavy, or dull and laborious? ... Ponderous.

gre.s: The biography's ____ prose, weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes, made it a chore to read despite the fascinating life it described.
gre.clue: weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes

example: Freight trains made a ponderous climb up the hill outside Srimangal, crawling past the tea gardens at walking speed.

en: To push someone or something down to a lesser place
hook: RELEGATE: sent back to the LEAGUE below.
story: Relegate. To push someone or something down to a lesser place. For thirty years, Grandfather's wooden radio stood proudly in the middle of the drawing room. The whole family gathered around it for news and cricket commentary. Then a big flat television arrived, and the radio was relegated to a dusty shelf in the storeroom. But every evening, Grandfather quietly carries it back to his room to listen to old songs. In football, a weak team is relegated, sent down to a lower league. So, what verb means to move something to a lower, less important position? ... Relegate.

gre.s: Although she was once celebrated as a pioneer, younger scholars now tend to ____ her work to footnotes, considering her methods hopelessly outdated.
gre.clue: considering her methods hopelessly outdated

example: Once the new laptops arrived, the old desktop computers were relegated to a dusty storeroom behind the canteen.

en: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to reject
hook: REPUDIATE: REPEL and DENY.
story: Repudiate. To refuse to accept or be associated with something; to reject it. One morning, Professor Hasan found a fake quote, printed beside his photo, spreading across social media. It praised a scheme he had never heard of. By noon he had posted a firm statement: he had never said those words, and he rejected everything they stood for. He had publicly repudiated the quote. In ancient Rome, to repudiate meant to divorce: to cast someone off and refuse all connection. So, what verb means to reject something and refuse any connection with it? ... Repudiate.

gre.s: Hoping to save his career, the candidate was quick to ____ the extremist group that had endorsed him, insisting he shared none of its views.
gre.clue: insisting he shared none of its views

example: In later life, the philosopher repudiated many ideas from his first book, calling them the errors of youth.

en: A speech in a play where one character thinks aloud while alone
hook: SOLI-LOQUY: SOLO speech (loqui = speak).
story: Soliloquy. A speech in a play where one character, alone on stage, thinks aloud. At a drama festival in Dhaka, the lights dimmed until only one spotlight remained. Tahmid stood in it, alone, playing Hamlet. He spoke softly, as if to himself: "To be, or not to be." The hall was so quiet you could hear the fans. When the soliloquy ended, the audience burst into applause. Soli means alone, as in solo, and loquy means speaking, as in eloquent: a soliloquy is speaking alone. So, what do you call a speech a character makes alone, thinking aloud? ... Soliloquy.

gre.s: Unlike a dialogue, in which characters respond to one another, a ____ lets the audience overhear a character's private reflections while he stands alone on stage.
gre.clue: while he stands alone on stage

example: In Macbeth's dagger soliloquy, the audience watches a man wrestle aloud with his own conscience on the eve of murder.

en: Seeming true or reasonable on the surface but actually false
hook: SPECIOUS: looks SPECIAL on the surface, but it's wrong underneath.
story: Specious. Seeming true or reasonable on the surface, but actually false. Tanjim told his mother he should skip his maths tuition. "Einstein failed maths at school, and look how he turned out." It sounded clever. His mother looked up from her sewing. "Einstein never failed maths. That story is a myth." Tanjim [laugh] had no answer. His argument was specious: attractive on the surface, hollow inside. Specious comes from the Latin species, meaning appearance; a specious claim only looks right. So, what word describes reasoning that looks sound but is actually false? ... Specious.

gre.s: The argument appeared persuasive at first, but on closer inspection its reasoning proved ____, resting on a statistic that had been misread.
gre.clue: resting on a statistic that had been misread

example: The salesman's specious claim that the filter removed every virus fell apart as soon as a chemist tested it.

en: Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy
hook: TEMPESTUOUS: like a TEMPEST (violent storm).
story: Tempestuous. Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy. Every spring, the kalbaishakhi storm rolls over the villages of Bangladesh: black clouds, sudden wind, mango branches cracking. Then, just as fast, the sky clears. Mou's friendship with her cousin Rima is just like that. They fight, cry, and refuse to speak for days, then share a plate of fuchka [laugh] as if nothing happened. Their friendship is tempestuous. Tempestuous comes from tempest, a violent storm, and a tempestuous bond blows hot and cold just as suddenly. So, what word describes a relationship full of stormy emotions? ... Tempestuous.

gre.s: The composer's ____ relationship with his patron, marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations, inspired several of his most passionate works.
gre.clue: marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations

example: The tempestuous final session of parliament ended with members shouting and tearing up copies of the budget.

en: Polished, sophisticated, and courteous
hook: URBANE: URBAN, city-polished manners.
story: Urbane. Polished, sophisticated and courteous. At a crowded wedding reception in Gulshan, Sharif uncle, a retired diplomat, moved through the hall greeting everyone by name. He chatted easily with the cooks, spoke smooth English with the foreign guests,. When a nervous waiter spilled tea on his sleeve, he only smiled and put the boy at ease. Everyone agreed he was the most urbane man in the room. Urbane and urban come from the same Latin word for city: urbane manners are the polish of city life. So, what word describes someone smooth, polished and courteous? ... Urbane.

gre.s: The ____ host, polished and witty, put even his most awkward guests at ease.
gre.clue: polished and witty

example: The urbane museum director chatted in French with the visiting minister and then in Bangla with the guards.

en: Remaining as a small trace of something that once was larger or more important
hook: VESTIGIAL: a VESTIGE, a remnant.
story: Vestigial. Remaining as a small trace of something that was once larger or more important. In biology class, Arifa's teacher pointed to the base of a human skeleton. "This small bone is the tailbone, a vestigial tail left from our distant ancestors." The class stared in wonder. Walking home past the crumbling gate of an old zamindar's palace, Arifa thought the gate was vestigial too, all that remained of a vanished estate. A vestige is a trace or remnant, so something vestigial is a leftover trace. So, what word describes a small leftover trace of something once larger? ... Vestigial.

gre.s: Although the office of governor-general still exists, its powers are now largely ____: the post survives as a ceremonial remnant of an era when it truly governed.
gre.clue: survives as a ceremonial remnant

example: The town's vestigial city wall, now a few crumbling stretches, still marks where the medieval market once stood.
